newsitem.title: THAILAND: Son says he understands Sihanouk's abdication offer.
newsitem.headline: Son says he understands Sihanouk's abdication offer.

text.p: Cambodia's ousted prime minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Monday he understood his father's offer to abdicate as an expression of dispproval of Hun Sen's power grab in Phnom Penh.
King Norodom Sihanouk said earlier on Monday that he was ready to abdicate as soon as he could be sure Cambodian leader Hun Sen would not criticise him for doing so.

"It is clear that it must be that the king as father of the Cambodian people cannot be happy with the coup d'etat, with the very serious setback for human rights and serious violation of human rights and with the political situation and political instability," he told a news conference.

"We are stepping into an era of great instability if not a civil war, so I understand very well the feeling and stance of my father His Majesty the King when he is talking about the possibility of abdicating," he added.
Sihanouk has been in Beijing for medical treatment for several months.

Ranariddh and his supporters were removed from power by Hun Sen in a bloody coup on July 6. His forces have since been pushed back to a town straddling the Thai border in northwest Cambodia, which Thai military sources said may fall any day.
Opposition leader Sam Rainsy also told Reuters he approved of the king's move, saying it would force signatories to the 1991 Peace Accords to acknowledge the U.N. peace process had failed.
"He is totally right. It is his constitutional right to do so (abdicate)," he told Reuters in Bangkok.

Major western and Asian states signed the 1991 accords pledging to support the United Nations in bringing peace and elections to Cambodia after years of turmoil. Ranariddh won the 1993 polls but later agreed to share power with Hun Sen.
Ranariddh said he had been barred by Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh from visiting some 30,000 Cambodian refugees on the Thai border since his arrival here on Saturday.
His aides had earlier reported Ranariddh had gone straight to the Cambodian border upon his arrival in Bangkok.
Ranariddh denied his forces were about to lose the border town of O'Smach, where mortar and rocket fire was heard on Monday, and said he and his party FUNCINPEC was far from defeated.
He vowed to continue his political struggle by lobbying governments to rally support for a return to democracy.
"The resistance will continue. The political and military resistance will continue. But I am very sorry to say that I fear that governments and states are not very concerned about Cambodia.
"They are concerned about their own interests. Japan, ASEAN and so on are taking care of Cambodia because they really care about their own interests," he said.
Ranariddh said he expected to be briefed by foreign ministers of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) after Monday's ministerial meeting in Singapore.
